WIFI-001.prerequisites: Physical proximity to the target wireless environment. A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection (Atheros/Ralink chipset recommended). hostapd-mana or a similar rogue-AP toolkit (Wifiphisher, EAPHammer) able to run a captive portal. A DNS/DHCP service you control (dnsmasq is the usual choice) to hand out spoofed resolution. Written authorization explicitly covering rogue-AP deployment and traffic interception, since this test actively lures real end-user devices.
WIFI-001.whatItIs: An attacker sets up a fake WiFi access point with a login page that looks like a familiar one — a hotel, airport, or corporate guest-network sign-in. It's paired with a DNS server the attacker controls. Since the victim's device automatically trusts whatever DNS server the fake AP hands it, every website the device tries to look up — including the checks phones use to detect a captive portal — can be redirected to attacker-controlled content, usually a fake login page designed to steal credentials.
WIFI-001.rootCause: When a device connects to WiFi and gets its network settings (DHCP/DNS), nothing actually proves the access point is who it claims to be. The device just trusts it. So there's nothing stopping an attacker from pretending to be legitimate network infrastructure and inserting themselves in the middle.
WIFI-001.impact: The attacker controls the victim's DNS for as long as they stay connected. That allows transparent redirection to phishing pages harvesting corporate or personal credentials, silent delivery of a malicious 'required' update, and steering toward lookalike domains before encryption is ever established. One detail raises the real-world success rate considerably: captive portals are expected to intercept traffic before login, so users are already conditioned not to question redirects or certificate warnings at this exact moment.
stepsToIdentify: Survey in-scope SSIDs with airodump-ng/Kismet and flag any AP whose SSID matches a known guest/captive-portal network but whose BSSID, vendor OUI, or channel doesn't match the organization's documented AP inventory.
Associate to the suspected captive portal and inspect the DHCP offer for the DNS server IP; compare it against the organization's documented resolver addresses.

Attempt to resolve a domain that should not exist (e.g. a random subdomain) and see whether the rogue DNS returns a wildcard/sinkhole answer instead of NXDOMAIN, which indicates DNS hijacking is active.
Capture the captive portal's login page source and diff it against the legitimate portal's markup, looking for credential-exfiltration form actions pointing off-network.
Check whether the portal is served over HTTPS with a valid certificate for the expected hostname; a self-signed or mismatched certificate on a portal expecting sensitive input is a strong indicator.

Review whether client devices enforce 802.1X/WPA2-Enterprise for the real guest network — environments still relying on an unauthenticated open SSID plus a portal are inherently more susceptible to this class of rogue infrastructure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes rogue-AP deployment and interception of real client traffic before proceeding — this test actively affects bystander devices in range.
Clone the legitimate guest SSID's name and (where feasible) security type using hostapd-mana or Wifiphisher, broadcasting from a channel with a stronger signal than the genuine AP.

Configure dnsmasq on the rogue AP to answer authoritatively for all queries, either sinkholing every hostname to a controlled web server or selectively hijacking only the domains needed for the proof-of-concept.
Stand up a captive-portal page that visually matches the target's real portal, with the login form posting to a local logger instead of the real authentication backend.
Wait for a test client to associate (or de-authenticate a nominated test device from the legitimate AP to force reassociation), then confirm the client is issued the rogue DNS server via DHCP.

Demonstrate impact by capturing a submitted test credential and by redirecting a benign lookup (e.g. a company domain) to the attacker-controlled page, then immediately tear down the rogue AP and stop capturing real traffic.
Record channel, SSID, BSSID, DHCP lease details, and screenshots of the spoofed portal for the report; never retain captured credentials beyond what's needed to prove the finding.

variants: Windows/Android/iOS captive-portal detection URL hijacking, where only the OS's connectivity-check hostname is redirected so the device automatically opens an in-app browser to the phishing page.
Malicious firmware/update lure, where the hijacked DNS points software-update domains to an attacker-hosted binary instead of a credential page.
Partial hijack limited to specific corporate domains rather than a full sinkhole, used to make the attack harder to notice during a live test.
mitigation: Require WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X with EAP-TLS/PEAP against a trusted RADIUS server and certificate) for guest and corporate SSIDs instead of an open network plus captive portal.
Deploy 802.11w Protected Management Frames so rogue APs can't easily force reassociation via spoofed deauthentication.
Run continuous wireless intrusion detection (WIDS/WIPS) that alerts on SSID spoofing, unexpected BSSIDs broadcasting known SSIDs, and rogue DHCP/DNS servers on the wired side.
Serve captive portals exclusively over HTTPS with HSTS and a certificate clients can validate, and train users to expect a specific, verifiable domain rather than any device claiming the SSID.
Segment guest wireless VLANs so a rogue-AP compromise can't reach internal DNS/DHCP infrastructure, and monitor for unauthorized DHCP servers with DHCP snooping on wired switches.
Push mobile device management (MDM) configuration that pins expected captive-portal certificates/domains for managed corporate devices.
WIFI-001.mitigationClientFacing: When a device joins your guest network it accepts, without question, whatever address book that network hands it for finding websites. On this network that address book can be replaced, which lets an attacker silently send a user to a page of their choosing while the address in the browser still looks correct. Everything the user sees tells them they are in the right place. The fix is to make the network hand out only resolvers you control, block devices from using any other, and ensure the sign-in portal itself sits on a proper certificate for a name you own. This is configuration work on equipment you already have rather than new spend.

WIFI-002.prerequisites: A wireless adapter in monitor mode within radio range of the target site (no association required — this is entirely passive). Kismet or the aircrack-ng suite (airodump-ng) for capture. Written scope confirming that passive over-the-air reconnaissance in the vicinity of the client's premises is authorized, since signal from adjacent, out-of-scope organizations may also be received incidentally.
WIFI-002.whatItIs: WiFi beacon and management frames are broadcast in plain text on purpose — that's how a device finds and joins a network in the first place. But this also leaks information the organization might not want public: network names (even 'hidden' ones, which briefly show up anyway), the AP's brand and model, how many devices are connected and roaming around, and sometimes internal hostnames or usernames tucked into a device's request to rejoin a previously-known network.
WIFI-002.rootCause: WiFi's discovery process has to be readable by anyone before they even connect — that's simply how a device finds a network to join. The actual finding here isn't that this data is visible (it has to be); it's that the organization hasn't accounted for what that visibility reveals — physical layout, staffing patterns, internal naming conventions.
WIFI-002.impact: An attacker within range can build a picture of the target without ever touching the network. They learn the physical footprint, the working hours from when devices connect and disconnect, and the device inventory from how each one identifies itself. Client probe requests sometimes reveal which networks a device has joined before. This rarely causes harm on its own, so it is usually rated low, but it is worth recording as the precursor that makes an evil twin or a targeted social engineering pretext far more effective.
stepsToIdentify: Run a passive survey with airodump-ng or Kismet for the engagement window and log every BSSID/SSID observed, including hidden SSIDs that resolve once a client associates.

Extract client probe-request history from the capture to identify previously-associated SSIDs being broadcast by devices in range (e.g. an employee's phone probing for a prior employer's or home network's SSID).
Fingerprint AP vendor/model from OUI and 802.11 information elements, and cross-reference against known default-configuration weaknesses for that hardware.
Correlate client association counts over time against expected business hours to see whether occupancy/staffing patterns are inferable purely from wireless traffic volume.
Check whether SSID naming conventions leak organizational detail (department names, building/floor numbers, internal project codenames) beyond what's operationally necessary.
Note whether hidden-SSID configuration is in use as a (false) security control — hidden networks are trivially revealed the moment any client associates, and shouldn't be relied upon.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the passive-monitoring scope and duration with the client, including how to handle incidentally-captured signal from neighboring, out-of-scope organizations.
Place a monitor-mode adapter at a representative vantage point (public areas, parking lot, adjacent floors if accessible) and capture continuously for the agreed window.
Aggregate captured beacons and probes into a channel/SSID/BSSID inventory, tagging each with signal strength to approximate physical AP placement.

Extract and de-duplicate client probe-request SSID lists to build the previously-associated-network exposure list per device (report only aggregate/anonymized findings, not individual employee identities, unless the client specifically wants that mapped).
Summarize occupancy inference (client-count time series) as a business-impact talking point rather than a technical exploit, since this finding's value is almost entirely informational.

Cross-reference discovered AP hardware against CVE databases for that vendor/model as a lead-in to other findings (e.g. WPS, firmware-specific bugs) rather than treating this item as exploitable on its own.

variants: Hidden-SSID de-cloaking, where the SSID is revealed the instant any legitimate client associates or sends a directed probe.

Passive capture over a multi-day window to profile shift patterns and site occupancy from association counts, which supports timing a later physical or social-engineering attempt.
mitigation: Treat SSID hiding as an inconvenience rather than a security control — don't rely on it, and avoid embedding sensitive internal naming in SSIDs regardless of whether they're hidden.
Configure client devices to not auto-broadcast probe requests for saved networks where the platform supports randomized/passive scanning only.
Use enterprise mobility management to standardize and periodically audit SSID naming conventions across the estate.
Where physical footprint inference is a genuine concern (e.g. high-security facilities), consider RF shielding or reduced transmit power to limit signal leakage beyond the building perimeter.
Monitor for and periodically conduct your own passive surveys to understand what an external attacker would learn about the site before they do.
WIFI-002.mitigationClientFacing: Simply listening to the air around your building reveals a useful amount about your organisation — which equipment you run, how your sites and departments are named, roughly how many people are present and when, and in some cases which networks your staff's devices have previously joined and will try to rejoin. None of this requires connecting to anything, so there is nothing in your logs to show it happened. You cannot stop the broadcasting, since that is how wireless works, but you can reduce what it says: avoid network names that reveal departments, floors or equipment types, and be aware that an attacker planning a visit already knows your quiet hours.

WIFI-003.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection. hostapd-mana (Karma/MANA mode) or a similar toolkit that auto-responds to any SSID a client probes for. Written authorization covering active rogue-AP deployment, since real bystander/employee devices will associate automatically.
WIFI-003.whatItIs: Most phones and laptops constantly broadcast the names of every WiFi network they've ever joined, looking for a match to auto-reconnect to. A 'Karma' attack takes advantage of this: a rogue AP listens for those broadcasts and simply answers 'yes, that's me' to every single one. So any device that's ever joined an open or weak network — home WiFi, a coffee shop, an old job's guest network — will automatically and silently connect to the attacker's AP, thinking it's just reconnecting somewhere familiar.
WIFI-003.rootCause: A device decides whether to (re)connect based purely on the network's name matching one it already trusts — there's no actual proof that the AP answering is the same physical AP it connected to before. Combined with auto-reconnect being the default behavior, any AP that claims a familiar name wins the connection without the user noticing anything.
WIFI-003.impact: Employee devices associate to attacker infrastructure silently, with no user interaction at all. From there the attacker intercepts traffic, hijacks DNS, phishes credentials through a fake captive portal, and injects content into any unencrypted session. Because most devices do not prompt before reconnecting to a remembered network name, the victim has no indication that anything unusual happened.
stepsToIdentify: With authorization, run a passive capture to catalog probe-request SSIDs broadcast by devices in range, which shows how many devices are candidates for a Karma-style association and what SSID names would need to be answered.
Test whether corporate-issued devices are configured to auto-connect to open or WEP/WPA-Personal networks from their connection history, versus requiring explicit user approval for unknown networks.
Check MDM/endpoint policy for whether Wi-Fi Sense-style network sharing or auto-join for open networks is disabled by policy.
Determine whether the organization's own guest network is open (unauthenticated), since that configuration is itself impersonable by a Karma AP with no cryptographic difference from the real thing.

Assess whether client devices validate server certificates for any 802.1X-based network in their history, since MANA's more advanced mode can also answer for WPA2-Enterprise SSIDs if certificate validation is weak.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly permits an active Karma/MANA rogue AP that will cause real, unwitting device associations.
Configure hostapd-mana in loud (Karma) mode to answer every probed SSID, or in MANA mode to selectively respond only to a target list agreed with the client to limit bystander impact.
Broadcast from a position with strong signal relative to legitimate infrastructure and monitor for associations from nominated test devices or, where scope allows, any device.

Once a device associates, demonstrate impact via a benign proof-of-concept — e.g. serving a test page over the intercepted HTTP session or logging DNS queries — without altering or exfiltrating real user data beyond what's needed for evidence.
Immediately tear down the rogue AP once the finding is proven and stop any interception of real traffic.
Document which SSIDs were successfully impersonated and which devices associated (by MAC/vendor only, not personal identity) as evidence for the report.

mitigation: Disable auto-connect / auto-join for open and legacy-security networks on managed devices via MDM policy.
Require WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with full certificate validation for all corporate SSIDs so there's no equivalent open network for a Karma AP to trivially impersonate.
Educate users to manually forget open networks (coffee shops, hotels, airports) once no longer needed rather than leaving them in the device's preferred-network list indefinitely.
Deploy WIDS/WIPS capable of detecting Karma/MANA behavior (a single AP answering many distinct SSIDs from one BSSID is a strong signature).
Where feasible, disable client-side probe-request broadcasting for saved networks (passive-scan-only mode) to remove the information Karma attacks rely on.
WIFI-003.mitigationClientFacing: Phones and laptops remember the networks they have joined and will reconnect automatically when a network with that name appears. An attacker can simply answer 'yes, that's me' to whatever a passing device asks for, and the device joins without the user doing anything or noticing. Company devices found during testing behaved this way. Fix it through your device management rather than by asking staff to be careful: turn off automatic joining of open networks, remove old saved networks from the managed profile, and require that corporate wireless only connects when the network proves its identity with a certificate. That last setting is what makes an impersonated network fail rather than succeed.

WIFI-004.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection (aircrack-ng-compatible chipset). The aircrack-ng suite (aireplay-ng) or mdk4. Written authorization explicitly covering active denial-of-service testing against wireless clients/infrastructure, since this test will disrupt legitimate connectivity for anyone in range on the targeted BSSID.
WIFI-004.whatItIs: A 'deauth' frame is a WiFi management message that tells a device (or every device at once) to disconnect from the network. Unless a specific protection (called PMF, or 802.11w) is turned on and required, these messages aren't verified in any way — so anyone within radio range can forge one pretending to be the real access point and instantly kick real users off the network.
WIFI-004.rootCause: The original WiFi standard never added any way to verify these disconnect messages were genuinely sent by the real access point — it just assumed only legitimate equipment would send them. A newer protection (802.11w/PMF) fixes this, but it's frequently left off, or set to 'optional' for compatibility with older devices — which means it protects nothing in practice.
WIFI-004.impact: Repeated deauthentication keeps clients disconnected for as long as the attack runs. That denies service to users, and in operational technology or point-of-sale environments it causes direct business disruption. It is also a stepping stone rather than an end in itself: it forces a handshake capture for offline cracking, or pushes a client onto a nearby rogue access point. Its presence usually means the other wireless findings are more exploitable than they look.
stepsToIdentify: Check the AP's advertised RSN information element for the MFPC (management frame protection capable) and MFPR (required) bits to determine whether PMF is supported and enforced, not just supported.

With authorization, send a small number of deauthentication frames to a nominated test client and confirm whether the client actually drops association (rather than silently ignoring the unauthenticated frame, which would indicate PMF is enforcing rejection).
Review AP configuration for 802.11w mode — disabled, optional/capable, or required — since "optional" still allows an attacker to target any client that hasn't itself negotiated PMF.

Confirm whether legacy clients on the network (older IoT/embedded Wi-Fi devices) lack 802.11w support entirely, which forces the AP into optional mode and reintroduces the exposure for the whole network even if modern clients support PMF.
Check for WIDS/WIPS alerting on deauthentication frame floods as a compensating control if PMF cannot be enabled network-wide.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes active deauthentication testing and agree a tightly bounded time window and target list (specific test client MACs) to minimize disruption to real users.
Identify the target AP's BSSID and channel, and the client MAC to be deauthenticated (or use the broadcast address only if the client has explicitly authorized network-wide disruption).
Send a bounded number of deauthentication frames (e.g. 5-10) to the nominated client and observe whether it disconnects and how quickly it attempts to reassociate.
If demonstrating the handshake-capture pivot, capture the WPA2 4-way handshake generated during the forced reassociation for the related offline-cracking finding.
If demonstrating the rogue-AP pivot, confirm whether the deauthenticated client reassociates to a nearby Karma/Evil-Twin AP faster than it reconnects to the legitimate one.
Stop the attack immediately once the finding is proven; do not run continuous or broadcast deauthentication beyond the minimum needed for evidence.
Document whether PMF was present/enforced, the client's reconnection behavior, and any successful pivot to handshake capture or rogue-AP association.

variants: Disassociation frame flooding as a functionally equivalent alternative to deauthentication where the AP filters one but not the other.
Targeted single-client deauth used purely to force a handshake capture (a precursor to offline WPA2-PSK cracking) rather than a sustained denial-of-service.

mitigation: Enable and require (not just support) 802.11w Protected Management Frames on all APs and enforce it in client Wi-Fi profiles pushed via MDM.
Retire or isolate legacy clients that don't support 802.11w onto a separate SSID so they don't force the whole network into PMF-optional mode.
Deploy WIDS/WIPS with deauthentication/disassociation flood detection and alerting.
For business-critical wireless (POS, OT/ICS), maintain a wired fallback and incident-response runbook for sustained RF denial-of-service.
Periodically test PMF enforcement after any AP firmware upgrade or configuration change, since defaults sometimes reset to optional.
WIFI-004.mitigationClientFacing: Anyone within range can knock devices off your wireless network at will, using inexpensive equipment and without joining the network or knowing any password. On its own this is a nuisance; it matters because it is the standard opening move for a more serious attack, since a device thrown off a network will look for another one to join and can be steered onto an attacker's. It is also what an attacker uses if they want to interrupt whatever your business does over wireless. Enabling protected management frames on your controllers stops the common form of this, and it is a setting on equipment you already own.

WIFI-005.prerequisites: Access to the organization's wireless configuration standard/policy documentation or admin console for the guest network. No special tooling required beyond the ability to review AP/controller configuration and interview the team responsible for guest Wi-Fi administration.
WIFI-005.whatItIs: Guest WiFi networks usually use one shared password, displayed at the front desk or handed out by staff, that's supposed to be changed periodically. This finding covers the case where that password rotation either doesn't happen, happens too rarely, or isn't tracked at all — so a password that leaked (a past visitor shared it, a former employee remembers it, someone posted it online) keeps working indefinitely.
WIFI-005.rootCause: With one shared password for everyone, there's no way to tell who leaked it or revoke access from just one person — the only real protection is how quickly a leaked password stops working. Without an enforced rotation schedule, a leaked password essentially never expires, and any past leak becomes permanent, standing access.
WIFI-005.impact: Anyone who ever legitimately learned the passphrase keeps network access indefinitely — a past visitor, a contractor, a delivery driver, or an employee who has since left. A single disclosure through social engineering or shoulder surfing therefore has an unbounded window. How much that matters depends on segmentation: it may be only internet access, or it may be a real foothold if guest-to-internal separation is also weak.
stepsToIdentify: Ask the wireless/network team for the documented guest-PSK rotation policy and evidence of the last few rotation dates.
Check whether rotation is a manual, easily-skipped process or is enforced/reminded by the wireless controller's own scheduling features.
Determine how the current passphrase is distributed (printed cards, reception verbal handout, digital signage) and how many historical passphrases might plausibly still be circulating informally.
Confirm whether former employees/contractors who had access to the guest key have any reason to still know a still-valid current passphrase.
Cross-reference with the client-isolation and network-segmentation findings to establish the real-world impact ceiling if a stale passphrase is still in use.
exploitationSteps: This is primarily a policy/process finding rather than a technical exploit — the "exploitation" is demonstrating that a plausible historical passphrase (obtained through the client's own disclosure during the interview, or via authorized social engineering if in scope) still authenticates.
With the client's cooperation, obtain an intentionally aged/former passphrase they confirm was in use previously.
Attempt association to the guest SSID using the aged passphrase and confirm whether it is still accepted.
If accepted, demonstrate the resulting network access scope (internet-only vs. any internal reachability) as the business-impact evidence for the report.

Where social engineering is separately in scope, this finding can be paired with a pretext (e.g. posing as a past visitor) to show realistic acquisition of a stale credential, but that should be tracked as its own SOCIAL-domain finding rather than conflated here.

variants: No rotation policy at all versus a documented-but-unenforced policy that has silently lapsed.
Rotation performed but the same passphrase pattern/predictable increment is reused each cycle (e.g. season+year), which meaningfully weakens the benefit of rotating at all.
Rotation performed on the controller but never propagated to printed cards or digital signage, so reception continues to hand out the previous passphrase and staff keep it working by request.
A separate long-lived 'events' or 'contractor' SSID excluded from the rotation policy entirely, which becomes the practical way in once the main guest key changes.
mitigation: Adopt WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with per-user or per-device credentials for guest access where the environment allows, removing the shared-secret rotation problem entirely.
Where a shared PSK guest network must remain, enforce a documented rotation cadence (e.g. monthly) via the wireless controller's scheduling feature rather than manual process.
Avoid predictable passphrase patterns between rotations; use a password generator and a fresh random value each cycle.
Enforce client isolation and strict guest-to-internal network segmentation so the blast radius of a stale/leaked passphrase is bounded to internet access only.
Track and log guest-network authentication events so unusual usage patterns after a rotation are noticeable.
WIFI-005.mitigationClientFacing: Your guest wireless password has not changed on the schedule your policy sets out, and the password we tested still works. That means every visitor, contractor and former employee who has ever been given it still has access today. Because the password is deliberately shared widely, its strength is irrelevant — the only control is how often it changes and how little the guest network can reach. Set a rotation the team will realistically keep to and automate the reminder, make sure the new password actually reaches reception and any printed cards on the day it changes, and confirm the guest network can reach the internet and nothing else. The second point matters more than the first.

WIFI-006.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection. EAPHammer or hostapd-wpe to run a rogue WPA2-Enterprise AP that impersonates the RADIUS server. Written authorization covering active credential-harvesting against real employee devices, since success depends on unwitting client association.
WIFI-006.whatItIs: Enterprise WiFi (WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise) is supposed to prove the network's identity to the device using a server certificate, checked during login. If devices are set up to accept any certificate — or that check simply isn't configured — an attacker can set up a fake access point with the same network name and a fake login server. The device will complete the login process anyway, and hand over the user's password (or a crackable hash of it) straight to the attacker, with no warning shown.
WIFI-006.rootCause: This whole authentication scheme only works if the device actually checks the login server's certificate against a known, trusted one before sending credentials. If that check is left at whatever the device's default is — often no real check at all — instead of being explicitly configured to trust only the company's real certificate, the device can't tell a real login server from a fake one. At that point the 'secure' enterprise network is no more protected than an open one.
WIFI-006.impact: The attacker harvests domain credentials, or hashes that can be cracked offline. Those are frequently the same credentials used for VPN, email and single sign-on, which turns a wireless-only foothold into full account takeover. The victim usually sees nothing wrong, because the fake access point can pass the real authentication through to the legitimate server after capturing what it needs, so the connection simply succeeds as normal.
stepsToIdentify: Review the corporate Wi-Fi profile pushed via MDM/GPO for explicit CA pinning and expected server-identity (server name) validation settings, rather than relying on the OS's out-of-the-box defaults.

Interview the wireless team on whether EAP-TLS (mutual certificate auth) is used versus PEAP-MSCHAPv2 (password-based inner auth), since the latter is the higher-value target for credential harvesting.

With a test device configured to organizational defaults (not hardened by a security-aware tester), attempt to associate to a controlled rogue AP broadcasting the corporate SSID and observe whether a certificate-trust prompt appears or authentication proceeds silently.
Check whether legacy or BYOD devices on the network are exempt from the MDM-enforced Wi-Fi profile and therefore rely on manual, inconsistent configuration.
Confirm whether 802.11w/PMF is enabled, since a common precursor to this attack is deauthenticating a client off the legitimate AP to force reassociation to the rogue one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes standing up a rogue WPA2-Enterprise AP and harvesting credentials from real or nominated test devices.
Configure EAPHammer with a self-signed certificate and the target SSID/security type cloned from the legitimate network.
Broadcast the rogue AP with strong signal and, where authorized, deauthenticate a nominated test client from the legitimate AP to force reassociation.
When the test client's EAP session begins, capture the inner MSCHAPv2 challenge/response (PEAP) or observe cleartext credentials (EAP-TTLS/PAP configurations).
Attempt offline cracking of the captured MSCHAPv2 hash against a representative password list to demonstrate real-world crackability within the engagement's time budget.

Tear down the rogue AP immediately after proving the finding; do not retain harvested credentials beyond what's needed as evidence, and rotate/report any real (non-test) credential captured incidentally to the client immediately.

variants: EAP-TTLS/PAP configurations that leak the inner credential in cleartext rather than as an MSCHAPv2 challenge/response, removing the offline-cracking step entirely.
Man-in-the-middle relay mode, where the rogue AP proxies the captured credential through to the real RADIUS server in real time so the victim's connection still appears to succeed.

mitigation: Enforce EAP-TLS with mutual certificate authentication (client and server certificates) rather than password-based PEAP/EAP-TTLS wherever device provisioning allows it.
Explicitly configure and push, via MDM/GPO, CA pinning and expected RADIUS server-identity validation for the corporate Wi-Fi profile — never rely on OS defaults.
Enable 802.11w/PMF to make the deauthentication-based reassociation precursor harder to execute.
Deploy WIDS/WIPS capable of detecting rogue APs broadcasting the corporate SSID with a mismatched certificate fingerprint.
Rotate any credential confirmed or suspected to have been exposed to a rogue AP during testing or a real incident, and audit for reuse of that credential on VPN/SSO.
WIFI-006.mitigationClientFacing: An attacker can stand up a copy of your corporate wireless network and collect staff login details as devices try to join it. The devices try to join because they cannot tell the copy from the original — they were never configured to check. This is one of the most direct routes from the car park to a working set of domain credentials. The remedy is a device configuration change rather than user training: every managed device must be told exactly which certificate the real network presents, and be set to refuse anything else. Once that is deployed, an impersonated network simply fails to connect, and the failure is itself a useful warning sign.

WIFI-007.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection. Wireshark/tshark for RSN information-element inspection, and mdk4/aireplay-ng for frame-injection testing. Written authorization for active management-frame injection against the target BSSID.
WIFI-007.whatItIs: It's not just disconnect messages that can be faked — other WiFi management messages (used for things like signal-quality reporting or telling a device to switch to a different access point) are also unverified unless PMF (802.11w) is turned on. This means an attacker can forge these too, to mess with a device's roaming decisions, force unwanted power-saving or channel changes, or trick a device into moving to an access point the attacker controls.
WIFI-007.rootCause: PMF protects these messages using a key set up during login — but only once it's actually turned on and required, not just allowed. Where PMF is optional or unsupported, any nearby device can forge these messages pretending to be the real access point, with nothing stopping it.
WIFI-007.impact: Beyond the denial of service already covered by the deauthentication finding, forged management frames allow an attacker to manipulate roaming — steering victims toward a weaker or attacker-controlled access point. They can also disrupt timing-sensitive traffic such as voice and video calls. And they serve as a probe for implementation bugs in how a particular access point or client parses malformed frames.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm 802.11w status (disabled / capable-optional / required) via the RSN information element, distinct from simply checking the SSID's headline security type.
With authorization, inject a forged BSS Transition Management request toward a nominated test client and observe whether it attempts to roam to an attacker-specified BSSID.

Fuzz/inspect how the target AP and a sample client handle malformed or unexpected action-frame subtypes, watching for crashes, reboots, or unexpected disconnects (coordinate carefully — this can cause real outages).
Check whether all client device types on the network (including embedded/IoT Wi-Fi stacks) support 802.11w, since a single legacy device can force the AP to leave PMF in optional mode network-wide.
Confirm whether the controller sets PMF to optional rather than required, since optional leaves any client that does not negotiate it fully exposed while the network reports itself as protected.
Verify PMF state per-SSID rather than globally, because a corporate SSID is frequently hardened while a guest or IoT SSID on the same controller is left at the default.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes forged management-frame injection beyond simple deauthentication testing, given the higher potential for unintended disruption.
Capture a baseline set of legitimate action frames from the target BSSID to use as a template for crafted forgeries.
Inject a forged BSS Transition Management request toward a nominated test client, directing it toward a controlled rogue AP, and observe whether the client roams as instructed.
Where in scope, test forged disassociation/action frames against a small, agreed set of non-production test devices only.
Document which frame types were accepted without cryptographic verification and which the client/AP correctly rejected (indicating partial PMF enforcement).

examplePayloads.label: Inspect RSN IE for PMF capability/requirement
examplePayloads.command: tshark -i wlan0mon -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype==0x08' -T fields -e wlan.bssid -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpc -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpr

examplePayloads.label: Craft/replay a forged action frame with mdk4 (WIDS/beacon test mode as proxy for frame-injection capability)
Baseline capture of legitimate action frames for template comparison
Read the PMF capability and requirement bits directly from the RSN capabilities field
examplePayloads.command: tshark -i wlan0mon -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype==0x08 && wlan.ssid=="<target-ssid>"' -T fields -e wlan.ssid -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpc -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpr

examplePayloads.label: Confirm a disassociation frame is accepted by observing the client re-authenticate after injection

variants: Spoofed BSS Transition Management (steering) requests used to herd clients toward a rogue AP as a more surgical alternative to a blunt deauth flood.
Malformed action-frame fuzzing aimed at crashing a specific AP/driver implementation rather than simply disrupting association.
Channel Switch Announcement injection, which moves clients to a channel the real AP is not using and produces a denial of service that survives longer than a deauthentication burst.
Spoofed Quiet or Silence action frames, which suppress client transmission entirely and are usually unmonitored because they are a legitimate part of the standard.
mitigation: Enable and require 802.11w across all APs and enforce it in the pushed client Wi-Fi profile.
Keep AP firmware current, since many action-frame-parsing crash bugs are fixed in vendor patches rather than addressed by PMF alone.
Deploy WIDS/WIPS tuned to detect anomalous management-frame patterns beyond simple deauth floods (e.g. unexpected BSS Transition requests).
Segregate legacy, PMF-incapable devices onto an isolated SSID/VLAN so they don't force the primary network into PMF-optional mode.
WIFI-007.mitigationClientFacing: Certain wireless control messages are accepted by your network without any check that they came from a legitimate source, which lets someone nearby disconnect devices, move them to a channel that does not work, or steer them toward a network they control. The protection against this is part of the wireless standard and your equipment supports it, but it is currently either off or set to optional — and optional provides no protection to any device that does not ask for it. Move it to required on the networks that matter, checking each network name separately rather than assuming a global setting applies, and confirm your older devices can still connect before you enforce it everywhere.

WIFI-008.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection, positioned to observe roaming events between two APs in the same 802.11r mobility domain. Wireshark for FT (Fast Transition) frame analysis. Written authorization to trigger and capture client roaming events.
WIFI-008.whatItIs: Fast Roaming (802.11r) lets a device switch between access points on the same network quickly, by pre-calculating session keys instead of doing a full login each time. Some implementations have been found to mess up that key calculation, reusing the same key material across roams under certain conditions — which reopens a KRACK-style weakness (see WIFI-009) specifically in this fast-roaming shortcut, even on networks that are otherwise patched against the original KRACK bug.
WIFI-008.rootCause: Fast Roaming deliberately trades some handshake security for speed by calculating new keys ahead of time instead of from scratch. Bugs in exactly how that pre-calculated key gets reused during a roam can cause the same key to be used twice — which is the exact kind of mistake KRACK exploited in the regular handshake, just showing up here instead.
WIFI-008.impact: Where the flaw is present, an attacker can decrypt frames exchanged immediately after a fast roam, or have forged and replayed frames accepted because the replay counter was reset. The effect is functionally the same as KRACK, but confined to the roaming transition window. It also depends on specific access point or client firmware rather than on the protocol itself, so it affects far fewer deployments.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm 802.11r is enabled on the target network by checking the beacon/probe-response Mobility Domain information element.
Identify AP vendor/firmware version and cross-reference against published advisories for FT key-derivation or nonce-reuse bugs specific to that hardware/software combination.

With authorization, capture the FT authentication/reassociation frames during a real or induced roam (e.g. by walking a test device between two APs, or attenuating signal to force a roam) and inspect for nonce/replay-counter values repeating across sessions.
Check whether firmware is current against the vendor's advisory history for this class of bug — this finding is almost always a firmware-currency issue rather than a fundamental 802.11r design flaw.
Establish whether FT is offered over-the-air, over-the-DS, or both, since the two paths derive keys through different message flows and a vendor fix frequently lands on only one.
Confirm whether the deployment uses a single mobility domain across the whole estate, because a shared domain widens the consequence of any key-derivation weakness from one AP to all of them.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes triggering roaming events and capturing the resulting FT handshake traffic.
Position monitoring equipment to observe both APs involved in the roam and force a test client to roam (physical movement, signal attenuation, or an authorized band-steering trigger).
Capture the FT reassociation exchange and compare derived key/nonce material across multiple induced roams for repetition.
If repetition is observed, attempt to decrypt a sample of post-roam traffic using the reused key material as proof of concept, limited to the authorized test client's own traffic.
Document the specific AP/client firmware versions involved, since remediation here is almost always a vendor patch rather than a configuration change.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm 802.11r / Mobility Domain is enabled
Capture FT reassociation frames during an induced roam
Inspect nonce/replay counter fields across captured roams
Enumerate the mobility domain identifier advertised by every AP in the estate
examplePayloads.command: tshark -i wlan0mon -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype==0x08' -T fields -e wlan.ssid -e wlan.bssid -e wlan.mobility_domain.mdid | sort -u

examplePayloads.label: Force a roam on a test client so the FT exchange can be captured on demand

variants: Nonce reuse specific to the FT-over-DS (over the Distribution System) roaming path versus the over-the-air FT path, which some implementations handle differently.
Combined exploitation with a rogue AP that advertises the same mobility domain to lure a fast-transition-eligible client and attempt key material capture during the resulting handshake.
A rogue AP advertising the same mobility domain identifier, which invites a fast transition from a legitimate client and moves the exchange onto attacker-controlled hardware.
FT enabled on an SSID that also permits legacy clients, where the fallback path negotiates without the FT protections the deployment is assumed to provide.
mitigation: Apply vendor firmware updates promptly — this class of bug is consistently fixed via patch rather than requiring 802.11r to be disabled outright.
Where a specific AP model has a confirmed, unpatched FT key-reuse advisory, disable 802.11r on that hardware until a fix is available, accepting the roaming-latency tradeoff.
Monitor vendor security advisories specifically for Fast Transition / 802.11r implementation bugs, not just general Wi-Fi CVEs.
Periodically re-test roaming behavior after firmware upgrades to confirm the fix is actually effective rather than assuming patch notes are sufficient.
WIFI-008.mitigationClientFacing: Your wireless uses a fast-roaming feature so that devices moving around the building do not drop calls or sessions. The way keys are handled during those handovers has had a series of vendor security fixes, and the equipment here is behind on them. This is a patching finding rather than a design flaw: the feature is worth keeping and the answer is to bring the firmware current and stay current. Worth knowing for planning: because the same roaming domain is shared across the estate, a weakness in one place is not contained to one access point, so treat the firmware update as an estate-wide job rather than a site-by-site one.

WIFI-009.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection, positioned within range of the target AP and a client whose firmware/driver is unpatched against KRACK (CVE-2017-13077 and related CVEs). The krackattacks-scripts / krackattack test suite. Written authorization for active 4-way-handshake replay against a nominated test client.
WIFI-009.whatItIs: KRACK exploits a quirk in how WPA2 devices install their encryption key. During login, message 3 of the handshake can be resent by the access point if it doesn't hear a reply — normally just for reliability. But on vulnerable devices, each resend causes the device to reinstall the same key and reset its counter back to the start. Since WPA2's security depends on a key only ever being used with fresh counter values, an attacker who can trigger this reset (by blocking the device's reply and replaying message 3) can then read, and on some setups even tamper with or inject, encrypted traffic.
WIFI-009.rootCause: The original WiFi security standard didn't clearly say that a device should ignore a resent message 3 once it had already installed the key. So a lot of real implementations — especially Linux and Android devices — reinstalled the key and reset the counter every single time that message was resent, instead of only the first time.
WIFI-009.impact: On unpatched clients an attacker can decrypt traffic that was assumed to be protected. On networks using TKIP or GCMP they can forge and inject packets too, because those ciphers suffer more from the underlying nonce reuse than AES-based CCMP does. Variants affecting the group-key handshake and fast transition were identified as well. Today the exposure is confined almost entirely to unpatched legacy clients, since the major vendors shipped fixes shortly after disclosure.
stepsToIdentify: Inventory client Wi-Fi driver/firmware and OS patch levels across the wireless estate and cross-reference against the vendor advisory list published alongside the original KRACK disclosure (CVE-2017-13077 through CVE-2017-13088).
Prioritize embedded/IoT and long-lifecycle devices (older Android versions, unmanaged IoT Wi-Fi modules) since these are the most likely to still be unpatched years after disclosure.

With authorization, run the krackattacks-scripts test suite against a nominated test client to confirm practically whether the reinstallation/nonce-reuse condition is exploitable, rather than relying on version numbers alone.
Check whether the network uses TKIP or GCMP anywhere (legacy compatibility mode), since successful exploitation there additionally permits forgery/injection, not just decryption.
Confirm whether the AP side is patched as well as the client side, since the FT and group-key variants are AP-side issues while the original four-way handshake variant is client-side.
Identify any device on the estate that can no longer receive firmware updates, because for those the only available remediation is network segmentation or replacement rather than patching.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes active 4-way-handshake manipulation against a specific, nominated test client — this is not a passive check.
Use the krackattacks-scripts test tooling (or an equivalent implementation) to position as a channel-based man-in-the-middle between the test client and the legitimate AP.
Selectively block or delay the client's message-4 acknowledgment so the AP retransmits message 3, forcing the client to reinstall the session key with its nonce/replay counter reset.
Attempt to decrypt subsequent traffic from the client using the now-predictable, reused key/nonce state as proof of concept.
On TKIP/GCMP-cipher test setups only, additionally attempt frame forgery/injection to demonstrate the more severe variant where applicable.
Report the specific client OS/driver version confirmed vulnerable and confirm remediation is a vendor patch, not a Wi-Fi configuration change.

Capture the handshake exchange during the induced retransmission
Check client driver/version quickly for known-vulnerable stacks
examplePayloads.command: dmesg | grep -i wifi ; adb shell getprop ro.build.version.security_patch  # example for Android test devices

examplePayloads.label: Test a nominated client for the four-way handshake reinstallation variant
Test the group-key handshake variant, which affects broadcast traffic and is patched separately
Confirm whether the AP retransmits handshake message 3, which is the precondition for the attack
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r krack_test-01.cap -Y 'eapol.type==3' -T fields -e frame.number -e wlan.sa -e wlan.da -e eapol.replay_counter

variants: Group-key handshake reinstallation, a separate variant affecting broadcast/multicast traffic decryption rather than the primary unicast 4-way handshake.
802.11r Fast BSS Transition handshake reinstallation (see the related FT roaming-key-reuse finding, which covers this variant specifically).
PeerKey (TDLS) handshake reinstallation, affecting direct client-to-client links rather than the client-AP path.
mitigation: Patch all client devices, drivers, and APs to vendor-fixed versions; treat any device that cannot be patched (end-of-life IoT, embedded Wi-Fi modules) as needing network isolation.
Disable TKIP/GCMP compatibility modes and standardize on CCMP (AES) to reduce the severity ceiling of any residual, unpatched-client exposure.
Segment legacy/unpatchable IoT devices onto an isolated VLAN with no access to sensitive internal resources.
Track vendor security advisories for Wi-Fi driver/firmware CVEs as part of routine patch management, not just OS-level patching.
WIFI-009.mitigationClientFacing: A known weakness in how wireless encryption keys are set up allows someone nearby to decrypt traffic from an affected device. Fixes have been available for years, so the issue is not the flaw but the devices that never received the update — typically older handsets, embedded equipment and anything from a supplier that has stopped issuing firmware. Patch what can be patched, on access points as well as clients, since different parts of the problem are fixed on each side. For equipment that can no longer be updated, the remaining option is to place it on its own network segment that reaches only what it must, and to plan its replacement.

WIFI-010.prerequisites: A wireless adapter in monitor mode within range of the target open network. Wireshark/tcpdump for traffic capture — no cracking or injection capability needed since the network carries no link-layer encryption at all. Written authorization to passively capture traffic traversing the open SSID.
WIFI-010.whatItIs: An open WiFi network has zero encryption — anyone nearby can quietly capture and read everything every connected device sends and receives, without needing to log in, guess a password, or actively attack anything at all.
WIFI-010.rootCause: The network was set up with no security type at all, instead of at least WPA2 or WPA3. This isn't a broken protocol — it's simply the absence of one, by configuration choice or oversight.
WIFI-010.impact: Any unencrypted application traffic is readable by anyone nearby — plain web traffic, unencrypted DNS, legacy mail protocols, internal plaintext protocols. That exposes credentials, session cookies and business data directly. Even where clients use encryption for the sensitive parts, metadata still leaks: which hosts they contact, how much data moves, and when. The absence of link-layer encryption also removes any barrier to active interception once an attacker has associated.
stepsToIdentify: Survey in-scope SSIDs and confirm authentication/encryption type from the beacon frame (Open vs WEP/WPA/WPA2/WPA3) using airodump-ng or a Wi-Fi scanner.
Associate to any open SSID found in scope and passively capture traffic to confirm frames are unencrypted and readable.
Identify what proportion of captured traffic is itself unencrypted at the application layer (plain HTTP, legacy protocols) versus TLS-protected, to size the practical impact.
Determine the business purpose of the open network (public guest access, IoT provisioning, legacy equipment) since remediation approach differs by use case.
Check whether the open network has any compensating network-layer isolation (client isolation, restricted routing) that limits impact even though link-layer confidentiality is absent.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes passive capture of traffic traversing the identified open SSID.
Associate a test device (or simply monitor passively without associating, since no association is required to capture frames on an open network) to the target SSID's channel.
Capture traffic for an agreed window and filter for cleartext credentials, session tokens, or sensitive data in transit as proof of concept.
Where legitimate test traffic is available, demonstrate session-cookie or credential capture from a nominated test account rather than intercepting real user data.

Document the proportion of unencrypted-at-the-application-layer traffic observed as the primary business-impact evidence, since this is usually the most persuasive finding for remediation prioritization.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm SSID security type from beacon
examplePayloads.command: airodump-ng wlan0mon  # ENC column shows OPN for open networks

examplePayloads.label: Passive capture without associating
Extract cleartext HTTP credentials from a capture (test traffic only)
Recover cleartext credentials and session cookies from a capture taken on the open network
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r open_net_capture.pcap -Y 'http.authorization || http.cookie' -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.authorization -e http.cookie

examplePayloads.label: Confirm whether client isolation is enforced by attempting to reach a second associated test host
examplePayloads.command: arp-scan --interface=wlan0 --localnet && nmap -sn $(ip -4 route show dev wlan0 | awk '/proto kernel/{print $1}')

variants: Open network paired with a captive portal (see the related rogue-DNS-via-captive-portal finding), where authentication happens at the portal but link-layer traffic remains unencrypted regardless.
Open network intended only for IoT provisioning that has since been left permanently accessible beyond its original provisioning window.
An open SSID retained solely for a printer or legacy handset that now provides an unauthenticated foothold onto a segment reachable from the corporate VLAN.
An enhanced-open (OWE) network misreported internally as encrypted, which does encrypt the air link but still authenticates nobody, so association control is absent despite the encryption claim.
mitigation: Migrate the SSID to WPA2/WPA3-Personal at minimum, or WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise for corporate use cases, so link-layer encryption is restored.

Where an open network is operationally required (public guest access with a captive portal), enforce client isolation and route all traffic through a filtering/monitoring proxy, and encourage clients to use a VPN.
Enforce HTTPS-only application design and HSTS so that even without link-layer encryption, application data in transit is protected end-to-end.
Segregate IoT-provisioning-only open networks with a strict time-bounded availability window rather than leaving them permanently active.
WIFI-010.mitigationClientFacing: One of your wireless networks has no encryption at all, so everything sent over it can be read by anyone within range using freely available software, with no password needed and no trace left behind. Even where the applications in use add their own protection, enough remains visible to be useful. If this network exists for visitors, replace it with one that encrypts the air link while still being easy to join; if it exists for a printer or some older equipment, the answer is to move that equipment onto a properly protected network or isolate it entirely. Either way, confirm that devices on it cannot see each other or reach anything internal.

WIFI-011.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection. The aircrack-ng suite (airodump-ng, aireplay-ng, aircrack-ng). Written authorization to capture and crack the target's WEP key, since this test recovers a live production key.
WIFI-011.whatItIs: WEP, the oldest WiFi encryption standard, uses a very short random value (24 bits) that gets sent in plain text with every single piece of data. Because that value is so small, it repeats constantly on a busy network — and once it repeats enough times, an attacker who's just quietly listening (or, faster, actively replaying traffic to speed things up) can mathematically recover the WiFi password within minutes, no matter how long or complex it is.
WIFI-011.rootCause: WEP's random value is fundamentally too small — it's guaranteed to start repeating after roughly 5,000 packets on a busy network — and it gets reused without any protection against that repetition being exploited. This isn't a settings mistake; it's a flaw baked into the protocol itself. There's no way to configure WEP to be secure — it can only be replaced with something newer.
WIFI-011.impact: The attacker recovers the WEP key completely, giving them the same network access as a legitimate client. They can also retrospectively decrypt any traffic captured earlier, once the key is known. Given how fast WEP falls — often under five minutes of active traffic — a WEP-secured network should be treated as effectively unauthenticated when rating risk.
stepsToIdentify: Survey in-scope SSIDs and flag any advertising WEP encryption in the beacon frame — this alone is sufficient to raise a critical finding without further testing being strictly necessary to prove impact.
Confirm the network is in active production use (versus a legacy/decommissioned AP left broadcasting) to correctly scope business impact.
Identify what's reachable from the WEP-secured segment (flat network vs. isolated VLAN) to size the blast radius beyond simple network access.

Where the SSID naming pattern suggests IoT or legacy operational technology (e.g. a distinct 'guest-legacy' or vendor-default SSID style), flag this specifically, since WEP is frequently retained on such devices even after being fully retired from the main corporate WLAN.

Establish whether the WEP network bridges onto the same VLAN as any production system, since a legacy AP on an isolated segment is a materially different finding from one bridged to the corporate network.
Identify what still requires WEP, because the finding is closed by replacing or isolating those devices rather than by reconfiguring the access point.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes recovering the live WEP key.
Start a targeted capture on the AP's BSSID and channel to collect data frames containing usable IVs.
If traffic volume is low, actively regenerate ARP request/response traffic via a replay attack to accelerate IV collection rather than waiting passively.
Run the PTW or FMS/KoreK statistical attack against the captured IVs once a sufficient count has been collected (typically tens of thousands of unique IVs).
Confirm the recovered key by associating a test device to the network using it, then immediately report the finding — do not use the recovered access beyond what's needed to prove the key is valid.

examplePayloads.label: Targeted capture of the WEP-secured BSSID
Accelerate IV collection via ARP replay
Recover the key from captured IVs
Recover the key from a low-traffic network using the fragmentation attack to generate keystream

variants: Shared-key authentication bypass, where the WEP challenge-response itself can be used to derive keystream without needing to crack the key first, enabling injection even before full key recovery.
Fragmentation attack, an alternative keystream-recovery technique usable when little legitimate traffic is available to replay.
Caffe Latte attack, which recovers the key from an isolated client that is merely in range of a spoofed SSID, without the real access point being present at all.
Retrospective decryption of previously captured traffic once the key is recovered, which extends the impact backwards to every session captured before the test.
mitigation: Migrate immediately to WPA2 or WPA3 — there is no configuration-level mitigation for WEP; the protocol must be replaced entirely.
Audit the estate for any remaining legacy hardware that only supports WEP (older barcode scanners, industrial equipment) and plan hardware replacement or network isolation as an interim measure.
Where legacy WEP-only devices cannot be replaced immediately, isolate them on a dedicated VLAN with no access to sensitive resources and treat the segment as untrusted.
Replace the access points or client devices that require WEP; the protocol has no secure configuration and disabling it at the controller is the only supported remediation path.
Where a device genuinely cannot be replaced within the remediation window, move it to a dedicated VLAN with no route to any production segment and restrict it to the specific destinations it needs.
WIFI-011.mitigationClientFacing: This network uses WEP, a protection standard broken beyond repair and formally withdrawn. The password can be recovered in minutes by anyone within range, regardless of how long or complex it is, because the weakness is in the standard itself and no setting makes it safe. Anything previously captured can also be decrypted retrospectively once that password is recovered. There is no configuration fix. The equipment requiring WEP must be replaced, and until it is, it must be moved onto an isolated network with no route to anything else you run. We would treat this as the highest-priority item in the wireless section of this report.

WIFI-012.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection. hcxdumptool/hcxpcapngtool and hashcat (GPU-accelerated) for offline cracking, or aircrack-ng with a wordlist. Written authorization to capture and offline-crack the WPA2-PSK handshake.
WIFI-012.whatItIs: Personal WiFi security (WPA2/WPA3-Personal) is built around one shared password used by every device on the network. If that password is short, a common word, or reused from somewhere else, an attacker who captures a single login handshake (or a related shortcut value called a PMKID) can crack it offline using GPU hardware — fast, and without ever being detected on the actual network while cracking.
WIFI-012.rootCause: The whole security of this setup rests entirely on how hard the shared password is to guess, since it's the only secret involved. There's no per-user login, and once an attacker has the handshake, there's no way to rate-limit their guessing since it all happens offline. A weak or reused password turns what should be uncrackable into something crackable in minutes to hours.
WIFI-012.impact: Once the passphrase is recovered the attacker has the same access as any legitimate client, plus the ability to decrypt traffic captured earlier. Because the cracking happens offline, there is no lockout and no limit on attempts. A passphrase reused across multiple sites, which is common with franchise or multi-site guest networks, multiplies the value of one successful crack considerably.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the network uses WPA2/WPA3-Personal (PSK) rather than -Enterprise, since this finding doesn't apply to per-user 802.1X authentication.
Interview the wireless team on passphrase complexity policy, rotation cadence, and whether the same passphrase is reused across multiple sites.

With authorization, capture a handshake or PMKID and attempt cracking against a curated wordlist (including the organization's likely naming conventions, not just generic dictionaries) within an agreed time/compute budget to estimate real-world crackability.
Check whether the passphrase follows an inferable pattern from publicly available information (company name + year, address, common defaults).
Determine whether the same PSK is configured across sites, franchises or tenants, because that turns a single recovered key into estate-wide access.
Establish how the PSK is distributed and how many people have held it, since a key known to departed staff is compromised regardless of its entropy.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes capturing a live handshake/PMKID and offline-cracking the recovered material.
Capture the 4-way handshake for the target BSSID, either passively or by triggering reassociation via a bounded, authorized deauthentication of a test client.

Convert the capture to hashcat format and run a GPU-accelerated dictionary/rule-based attack using a wordlist tailored to the organization's likely conventions, escalating to a broader dictionary if time/compute budget allows.
If successful, confirm the recovered passphrase by associating a test device, then stop — don't pivot into the live network beyond what's needed to prove impact.

Where cracking doesn't succeed within the engagement's time budget, report the passphrase as "not trivially crackable within X GPU-hours" rather than claiming it is strong, since this is a time-bounded rather than absolute conclusion.

examplePayloads.label: Capture handshake for the target BSSID
Convert capture for hashcat
GPU-accelerated dictionary + rule attack
Aircrack-ng alternative against a curated wordlist

variants: PMKID-based cracking (clientless, see the dedicated PMKID finding), which removes the need to capture a full 4-way handshake or trigger client reassociation at all.
Passphrase reuse across multiple physical sites or franchise locations, where a single successful crack compromises every site using the same value.
A high-entropy passphrase undermined by being stored in a shared document or MDM profile readable by every enrolled user, which defeats the entropy entirely.
Identity PSK (iPSK) deployed but with a shared fallback key left enabled for onboarding, which reintroduces the single-key weakness the feature exists to remove.
mitigation: Enforce a long, high-entropy, randomly generated passphrase (20+ characters) rather than a memorable phrase, and store it in a password manager for distribution rather than relying on staff memorization.
Migrate to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with per-user credentials wherever the environment supports it, removing the shared-secret cracking risk entirely.
Never reuse the same PSK across multiple sites or with any other system's credentials.
Rotate the passphrase on a defined cadence and immediately upon any suspected disclosure or staff turnover with knowledge of it.
Where WPA3-Personal (SAE) is supported by all clients, prefer it over WPA2-PSK, since SAE's handshake resists offline dictionary attacks even against weaker passphrases.
WIFI-012.mitigationClientFacing: The same wireless password is used across a wide part of your estate, and everyone who has ever needed it still knows it. That includes people who have left. Because one password protects everything, a single disclosure — a leaver, a shared document, a photograph of a whiteboard — opens every site at once, and changing it means touching every device that uses it, which is why it rarely gets changed. The durable fix is to move corporate wireless onto individual logins, so access can be removed for one person without affecting anyone else. Where that is not yet practical, at minimum use a different password per site so one disclosure does not compromise all of them.

WIFI-013.prerequisites: A wireless adapter in monitor mode within range of the target devices. Kismet or a custom capture/analysis script for probe-request fingerprinting. Written authorization for passive tracking analysis of devices in the vicinity.
WIFI-013.whatItIs: Phones now randomize the WiFi address they broadcast while searching for networks, specifically to stop people from tracking a device over time. But several real-world flaws have let attackers defeat this anyway: message sequence numbers that stay consistent across address changes, a device's other broadcast details (supported speeds, capabilities) forming a unique 'fingerprint' regardless of address, and on some older phones, briefly falling back to the real address under specific conditions.
WIFI-013.rootCause: Randomizing the address only hides one piece of information. If everything else about the device's broadcasts stays the same and predictable — the order of fields, the sequence numbering pattern, the timing — an observer can still recognize 'this is the same device' across every address change, without ever needing to know the real address. That defeats the whole point of randomizing it.
WIFI-013.impact: Individuals can still be tracked by movement and dwell time across a monitored area, despite their device correctly randomising its address. That covers retail analytics abuse, stalking, and corporate surveillance of employee movement. It undermines the privacy expectation users reasonably hold when the feature is enabled. This is usually a lower-severity informational finding, unless the organisation operates somewhere visitor or employee tracking is a stated concern.
stepsToIdentify: Capture probe requests from a nominated test device over a period covering at least one MAC randomization cycle (varies by OS/vendor).

Extract non-MAC fingerprint features (IE ordering, supported rate set, extended capabilities, vendor-specific IEs, sequence-number increment behavior) and check whether they remain stable across the observed MAC changes.
Attempt to cluster probes by fingerprint similarity alone (ignoring MAC address) and confirm whether the clustering correctly re-identifies the same test device across its randomized addresses.
Check the test device's OS/patch level against known public research on MAC-randomization bypass techniques for that platform and version.

Establish whether randomisation is per-network or per-session on the client platforms in use, since per-network randomisation keeps a stable address for the corporate SSID and provides no privacy at all on site.

Determine whether any deployed system deliberately depends on a stable client MAC — captive portals and MAC allowlists both do — because that dependency forces randomisation off and is usually the real root cause.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope and, where individuals other than nominated test devices might be incidentally observed, agree handling/retention limits for that data given its privacy sensitivity.
Capture probe-request traffic from a nominated test device across multiple randomization cycles (toggle Wi-Fi off/on, or wait for the OS's periodic rotation).
Build a fingerprint from stable, non-MAC fields and demonstrate successful re-identification of the same physical device across its changing MAC addresses.
Report the finding in aggregate/technical terms (fingerprint stability, re-identification success rate) rather than tracking or reporting on real bystanders' movement.

Where the fingerprint clustering has a false-positive rate high enough to be operationally unreliable, note this explicitly in the report as a partial-mitigation finding rather than a complete tracking-bypass capability.
