variants: EAP-FAST PAC file interception and reuse when provisioning is done insecurely (anonymous PAC provisioning).
RADIUS shared-secret brute forcing where a weak, guessable shared secret between the AP and RADIUS server allows an attacker with wired access to impersonate the RADIUS server directly.
MAB bypass combined with VLAN hopping once initial network access is obtained, extending impact beyond the isolated MAB segment.
mitigation: Enforce EAP-TLS with mutual certificate authentication as the sole permitted EAP method where feasible, disabling weaker methods like PEAP-MSCHAPv2 and EAP-FAST entirely.
Configure client supplicants to strictly validate the RADIUS server's certificate (including CA pinning) and refuse to connect to networks presenting an unrecognized or self-signed certificate.

Avoid MAB wherever possible; where required for legacy devices, isolate MAB-authenticated devices into a tightly restricted VLAN with no access to sensitive resources and monitor for MAC address anomalies (e.g. the same MAC appearing on multiple ports/locations simultaneously).
Use long, high-entropy RADIUS shared secrets and rotate them periodically.
WIFI-026.mitigationClientFacing: Your corporate wireless uses individual logins, which is the right design. Two gaps were found in how it is enforced. Weaker login methods remain available and an attacker can request one instead of the strong method, and there is an approved-device list that admits equipment by an identifier which can simply be copied. Disable the weaker methods on the authentication server so the strong one is the only option, and treat the device list as an inventory convenience rather than a security control — anything relying on it for access should be moved behind proper authentication.

WIFI-027.prerequisites: Written authorisation to transmit on the target site's RF environment, including agreement that a test access point may briefly broadcast an SSID resembling the corporate one. A wireless adapter capable of access-point mode. A named client contact in the security operations team who can confirm whether an alert was generated, since the entire finding depends on the defender's side rather than the attacker's. Physical presence at the site, or a cooperating on-site participant.
WIFI-027.whatItIs: Every offensive wireless technique in this domain assumes the attacker's transmitter goes unnoticed, and that assumption is almost never verified. This case tests it directly: stand up a controlled test access point and measure whether the organisation detects it, how long detection takes, whether anyone is alerted, and whether anyone acts. It is a detection and response finding rather than a vulnerability — the question is not whether a rogue AP can be created, which it always can, but whether the organisation would ever know.
WIFI-027.rootCause: Wireless intrusion detection is frequently either absent, deployed only at headquarters while branch sites are unmonitored, or present but generating alerts nobody reviews. Where a controller offers rogue detection as a feature it is often left at a default that classifies neighbouring networks as rogue too, producing enough noise that genuine detections are lost among them. The underlying reason is that wireless monitoring sits between the network and physical security teams and is frequently owned by neither.
WIFI-027.impact: Without detection, an evil twin, a Karma responder, or an unauthorised AP plugged into the corporate LAN can operate indefinitely. That converts every other wireless finding from a time-boxed opportunity into persistent access, and it removes the compensating control organisations typically cite when accepting the risk of a wireless weakness. It also means an employee-installed AP bypassing perimeter controls could sit on the network for months, which is the most common real-world occurrence of this issue and rarely malicious in intent.
stepsToIdentify: Establish whether a wireless intrusion detection or prevention capability exists at all, and whether it covers this specific site rather than only the primary office.
Determine how rogue classification is configured — whether it distinguishes an AP plugged into the corporate LAN from a neighbouring business's legitimate network.

Ask the security operations team what a rogue AP alert looks like on their side, and whether any have been raised in the past year, since a long silence usually indicates absent coverage rather than a clean environment.
Conduct a passive survey to inventory every AP visible at the site, and compare it against the organisation's own asset list — a mismatch is a finding before any transmission occurs.
Check whether wired-side controls (802.1X on access ports, port security) would independently prevent an unauthorised AP from being plugged in.
Confirm who is expected to respond to a detection and within what timeframe, since a detection nobody owns is functionally the same as no detection.
exploitationSteps: Agree the test SSID, its duration, the exact time window, and the halt procedure in writing before transmitting anything, and confirm no client devices are expected to join.
Start with the least intrusive variant: broadcast a distinctly-named test SSID that no employee device would ever auto-join, and measure whether it is detected.
Record the elapsed time between first transmission and any alert reaching a human, distinguishing detection by a system from detection by a person.
If the benign SSID goes unnoticed, escalate as agreed to an SSID resembling the corporate one, since detection frequently keys on name similarity — but keep the window short and monitored.
Do not allow real client devices to associate; use a fixed test client if association behaviour must be demonstrated at all.
Shut down the test AP at the agreed time regardless of outcome, confirm with the client that no residual alerts remain open, and report the detection time as the primary metric.

variants: Detection present but unowned, where the system raises an alert that reaches a queue nobody monitors — technically detected, operationally invisible.
Coverage gaps at branch or satellite sites while headquarters is monitored, which is the most common real-world pattern.
Alert fatigue where neighbouring businesses are classified as rogue, burying genuine detections in noise.
Detection without containment, where the system identifies a rogue AP but has no automated or procedural response to remove it.
mitigation: Deploy wireless intrusion detection covering every site where corporate wireless operates, not only the primary office.
Tune rogue classification to distinguish an AP bridged onto the corporate LAN from a neighbouring network, so alerts stay actionable.
Assign explicit ownership and a target response time for rogue AP alerts, since an unowned alert is equivalent to no detection.
Enforce 802.1X on wired access ports so an unauthorised AP cannot obtain network access even if it goes undetected over the air.
Maintain an accurate inventory of authorised access points, since rogue detection is only meaningful relative to a known-good baseline.
Rehearse the response: periodically stand up an authorised test AP and measure detection-to-response time as an operational metric rather than assuming the capability works.
WIFI-027.mitigationClientFacing: Every other wireless finding in this report assumes an attacker's equipment goes unnoticed, and we tested that assumption directly by operating a test access point on site. It was not detected, and no alert was raised. That matters because it changes the character of every other item here: without detection, a temporary opportunity becomes permanent access. It also means an access point plugged in by an employee for convenience — by far the most common real occurrence — could sit on your network indefinitely. Enable rogue detection on your controllers, tune it so neighbouring businesses do not drown out real alerts, and agree who responds.

WIFI-028.prerequisites: A wireless network advertised as WPA3 but operating in transition mode, where WPA2 clients are still accepted on the same SSID. A wireless adapter supporting monitor mode and packet injection. Written authorisation covering rogue access point deployment and offline handshake cracking, since the attack captures material from real clients.
WIFI-028.whatItIs: Transition mode exists so older clients keep working while an estate migrates, and it does that by accepting both WPA3-SAE and WPA2-PSK on one SSID. The security of the network therefore falls to WPA2 for any client that can be persuaded to use it. An attacker stands up a rogue access point advertising the same SSID with only WPA2 offered; a capable client associates using the weaker method and the resulting handshake is crackable offline. The organisation believes it deployed WPA3.
WIFI-028.rootCause: Transition mode is a compatibility compromise, and the protection SAE provides against offline dictionary attack only holds if SAE is actually used. Because both methods share one passphrase, breaking the WPA2 handshake yields the credential for the WPA3 network too. Most clients do not warn when they associate with the weaker method, and most deployments are left in transition mode indefinitely because nothing visibly breaks.
WIFI-028.impact: The offline dictionary resistance that motivated the WPA3 upgrade is lost entirely, and a weak passphrase becomes crackable exactly as it was before. Recovering the passphrase yields network access and, on a pre-shared key network, the ability to decrypt other clients' traffic where the handshake was observed. The organisation's own reporting will state that WPA3 is deployed, so the gap is unlikely to be found without wireless testing.
stepsToIdentify: Capture beacon and probe response frames and inspect the RSN element for the advertised authentication suites.
Determine whether both SAE and PSK appear, which is the definition of transition mode.
Check whether management frame protection is required or merely capable, since required PMF blocks the deauthentication step.
Inventory which clients on the estate actually support WPA3, to establish whether transition mode is still needed at all.
Review the controller configuration for transition mode settings and for any timeline to disable it.
Confirm whether the same passphrase is shared between the transition SSID and any other network.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the engagement scope permits rogue access point deployment and handshake capture from production clients.
Record the target's beacon configuration so the rogue access point matches the SSID and channel plan.
Stand up an access point advertising the same SSID with only WPA2-PSK offered.
Where PMF is not enforced, deauthenticate a target client to prompt reassociation; where it is enforced, document that this step is blocked.
Capture the resulting four-way handshake from any client that associates using WPA2.
Crack offline against a wordlist reflecting the organisation's likely passphrase style, and report the time taken as the measure of exposure.

variants: A client that prefers the stronger method but falls back when the rogue is closer, which makes signal strength the deciding factor.
WPA3-Enterprise transition mode, where the fallback is to WPA2-Enterprise and the target becomes EAP credentials rather than a passphrase.
Targeting only a subset of clients known to lack WPA3 support, avoiding the more visible broad deauthentication.
A passphrase shared with a guest or IoT network, so recovering it from the weaker network compromises the stronger one.
mitigation: Disable transition mode once client inventory confirms WPA3 support, and treat the migration as a task with a completion date rather than an indefinite state.
Require management frame protection, which removes the deauthentication step used to force reassociation.
Where transition mode must remain, place legacy clients on a separate SSID with its own passphrase and its own network segment.
Never share a passphrase between a transition SSID and any other network.
Use a long random passphrase so that even a captured WPA2 handshake is not practically crackable.
Deploy wireless intrusion detection capable of alerting on an SSID being advertised with weaker suites than the authorised configuration.
WIFI-028.mitigationClientFacing: Your wireless is configured to accept both the current WPA3 standard and the older WPA2 at once, so that older devices continue to work. An attacker can simply choose the older option, which means devices capable of the stronger protection do not receive it. This is a deliberate compatibility decision rather than a mistake, and the fix is a planning matter: identify which devices still require the older standard, replace or segregate them, and then turn the fallback off. Until that happens it is more accurate to describe this network as WPA2-protected than WPA3-protected, which is worth knowing if WPA3 has been cited in any compliance response.

WIFI-029.prerequisites: A guest or public network using Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, typically in transition mode where an open SSID is advertised alongside the encrypted one. A wireless adapter with monitor mode. Authorisation covering rogue access point deployment on a guest network, and agreement on whether guest traffic may be captured, since it may include non-employee users.
WIFI-029.whatItIs: OWE gives an open network encryption without a passphrase, which is a real improvement over a plain open network. Transition mode preserves compatibility by advertising a hidden open SSID alongside it, and clients that do not support OWE join the open one. An attacker advertising only the open variant collects clients whose traffic is then unencrypted. Users see the same network name they always join and have no indication which variant they landed on.
WIFI-029.rootCause: The transition design deliberately accepts an unencrypted fallback so that older clients keep working. Nothing in the client interface distinguishes an OWE association from an open one, so the user cannot tell and will not be warned. OWE also provides no authentication of the access point, meaning even a correct OWE association gives no assurance that the network is the intended one — it protects against passive interception, not against an adversary in the middle.
WIFI-029.impact: Guest traffic that the organisation believes is encrypted is transmitted in the clear for any client the attacker captures. Anything not protected by transport encryption above the link layer is readable, including plaintext protocols and metadata such as hostnames. Because guest networks commonly carry personal devices, the exposure often extends to non-employees, which changes the reporting obligations. The finding is also frequently missed because the controller reports OWE as enabled.
stepsToIdentify: Capture beacons and identify whether both an OWE SSID and an open transition SSID are present.
Inspect the OWE transition element in the beacon to confirm the pairing between the two SSIDs.
Associate a client that lacks OWE support and confirm it lands on the open variant with no user-visible warning.
Check whether the guest network enforces any form of captive portal authentication after association.
Determine whether client isolation is enabled on the guest network, since that limits what a captured client is exposed to.
Establish what the organisation believes is deployed, since the gap between belief and configuration is often the finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, and agree explicitly whether guest client traffic may be captured given that it may involve non-employees.
Record the target beacon configuration including the SSID pair and channel.
Advertise an open access point using the guest SSID, with no OWE element.
Observe which clients associate, and confirm from captured frames that the association is unencrypted.
Demonstrate visibility with metadata only — hostnames and plaintext requests — rather than capturing content, unless content capture is separately authorised.
Record how many clients preferred the rogue open network, as that number is what quantifies the exposure.

variants: A plain open network presented as secure because a captive portal is used, where the portal provides no link-layer encryption at all.
An adversary in the middle on a correct OWE association, since OWE authenticates nothing about the access point.
Downgrade targeting only clients whose probe behaviour indicates no OWE support, reducing visibility.
Guest network with no client isolation, so a captured client can also be reached directly by other associated devices.
mitigation: Move to OWE-only once client support allows, and treat the transition SSID as temporary with a review date.
Enable client isolation on guest networks so association does not grant reachability to other guests.
State plainly in guest-facing material that the network provides no authentication of the access point and that transport encryption remains the user's protection.
Deploy wireless intrusion detection to alert on the guest SSID being advertised by unauthorised hardware.
Where guest access carries any sensitivity, require per-user credentials rather than relying on OWE alone.
Keep guest traffic on a segment with no route to corporate resources, so a downgraded client cannot reach anything internal.
WIFI-029.mitigationClientFacing: Your guest network uses the newer standard that encrypts traffic without requiring a password, which is a genuine improvement over a fully open network. It is running in a compatibility mode that also accepts plain unencrypted connections, so a device can be pushed onto the unencrypted path and the benefit is lost. As with the corporate network, the fix is to establish which devices still need the fallback and then remove it. In the meantime, treat the guest network as unencrypted when deciding what it is allowed to reach, rather than relying on protection an attacker can opt out of.

WIFI-030.prerequisites: A guest wireless network alongside corporate wireless on the same infrastructure. Credentials or open access to the guest network, which is typically available from reception or a printed notice. Authorisation to scan from the guest segment toward internal ranges, with agreed target ranges and a defined stop point before any exploitation of a reachable service.
WIFI-030.whatItIs: Guest wireless is usually treated as a convenience rather than as a network boundary, and the configuration is often done once at installation and never reviewed. The question this case answers is narrow and practical: from a device on the guest network, what internal systems can actually be reached? Common findings are reachable management interfaces, a DNS or DHCP server answering from the corporate range, printers, and building systems that were placed on the wrong VLAN.
WIFI-030.rootCause: Segmentation is implemented on the wireless controller as a VLAN assignment and assumed to be enforced end to end, while the actual enforcement depends on firewall rules at the boundary that are frequently permissive or absent. Shared services such as DNS, NTP and print are deliberately exposed to guests for convenience, and each exposure is a path. Changes made for a specific need, such as a temporary contractor requirement, are rarely reverted.
WIFI-030.impact: An attacker needs only to be within wireless range and obtain a guest password that is often printed on a wall. From there, reachable internal services provide a foothold that bypasses every perimeter control the organisation operates. A reachable management interface on network hardware is the most serious common outcome, since default or weak credentials there yield control of the infrastructure that implements the segmentation in the first place.
stepsToIdentify: Obtain guest access through the normal route and record how easily it was obtained and whether it expires.
Determine the address assigned to a guest client, the gateway, and the DNS servers offered.
Establish whether the offered DNS resolver sits in the corporate range, which is a common and revealing misconfiguration.
Scan the guest segment first to determine whether client isolation is enforced between guests.
Probe agreed internal ranges to map what is reachable, distinguishing filtered from closed from open.
Identify the function of anything reachable, prioritising management interfaces, directory services and file shares.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope names the internal ranges that may be probed and the point at which testing stops.
Connect as an ordinary guest and capture the full DHCP offer including all options.
Test reachability of the gateway's own management interface, which is frequently exposed to the segment it serves.
Sweep the agreed internal ranges for responsive hosts and identify the services found.
For any management interface reached, confirm accessibility and stop at the login prompt rather than attempting credentials unless authorised.
Document each reachable service with the evidence that it was reached from the guest segment specifically.

variants: Guest and corporate traffic sharing a VLAN entirely, where separation exists only as an SSID name.
A captive portal that assigns the corporate VLAN before authentication completes.
IoT or building management systems placed on the guest VLAN, reachable by any guest.
A guest network with a route to the internet through the corporate proxy, exposing internal proxy configuration and authentication.
mitigation: Terminate guest traffic on a dedicated VLAN with a default-deny egress rule toward all internal ranges.
Provide guest DNS from a resolver dedicated to that segment rather than from a corporate server.
Enable client isolation on the guest network so guests cannot reach each other.
Bind management interfaces to a dedicated management network and deny access from user or guest segments.
Rotate guest credentials on a schedule and prefer per-visitor vouchers over a shared printed password.
Test segmentation from the guest network itself on a recurring basis, since configuration drift is the usual cause here.
WIFI-030.mitigationClientFacing: Guest and corporate wireless are intended to be separate, and they are not fully. From the guest network it was possible to reach systems that should only be reachable internally. This matters more than any individual wireless weakness, because the guest network is deliberately easy to join — that is its purpose — so anything reachable from it is effectively reachable by anyone who can sit in your reception area or car park. Tighten the separation at the firewall so that guest traffic can reach the internet and nothing else, then re-test rather than assuming the rule change worked, since these paths are frequently reopened by a later, unrelated change.

WIFI-031.prerequisites: Corporate endpoints with wireless adapters capable of acting as an access point, which covers essentially all current laptops. A wireless adapter with monitor mode for discovery. Authorisation to survey and to associate with any unauthorised access point found, and agreement on whether the endpoint behind it may be examined.
WIFI-031.whatItIs: An employee who turns on a mobile hotspot, or connects to a phone's tethered network while docked, creates a path from outside the network straight onto a machine that is inside it. The bridge is built by a trusted user for an ordinary reason such as poor coverage or a blocked site. Nothing malicious happens, and the organisation's perimeter now has an undocumented opening for as long as the adapter stays on.
WIFI-031.rootCause: Operating systems let a standard user enable hotspot and ad-hoc modes without administrative rights, because the feature is aimed at consumers. Endpoint configuration baselines frequently omit the setting because it is not obviously security-relevant. Wireless intrusion detection, where deployed, is usually tuned to find rogue access points advertising corporate SSIDs and will not flag a laptop broadcasting a personal network name.
WIFI-031.impact: A bridged endpoint gives an attacker within wireless range a route onto a domain-joined machine while bypassing the perimeter firewall, proxy and inspection entirely. If the endpoint is simultaneously on the wired network, the bridge may extend further inward depending on routing and forwarding configuration. Tethered connections also remove the organisation's visibility of that machine's traffic completely, so any compromise that occurs over the tether is invisible to network monitoring.
stepsToIdentify: Survey the premises for access points advertising SSIDs outside the authorised set, including default phone and laptop hotspot names.
Correlate the MAC address prefixes of unknown access points against vendor ranges typical of laptops and phones.
Check endpoint configuration policy for any restriction on hotspot, ad-hoc and Wi-Fi Direct modes.
Look for endpoints with two active network interfaces simultaneously, which indicates a potential bridge.
Review whether wireless intrusion detection alerts on any unauthorised access point or only on SSID impersonation.
Assess whether endpoint telemetry would show traffic that bypassed the corporate network path.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers surveying and associating with unauthorised access points discovered on site.
Conduct a walkthrough survey during working hours, since these networks appear and disappear with user activity.
Record each unauthorised access point with its SSID, BSSID, encryption and approximate location.
Associate where permitted and determine whether the host offers any service or routes toward internal addresses.
Establish whether the host is simultaneously connected to the corporate network, since that is what makes it a bridge.
Stop at demonstrating the bridge and report per device, since remediation is per endpoint and per policy.

variants: A phone tether used while the laptop remains on the wired network, creating the bridge without any laptop-hosted access point.
Wi-Fi Direct connections to printers and displays, which create ad-hoc links that inventory rarely covers.
A USB cellular modem, which produces the same bypass with no wireless signal to survey for.
A deliberately placed rogue access point plugged into a wall port, which presents similarly in a survey but is an intrusion rather than user behaviour.
mitigation: Disable hosted network, hotspot and ad-hoc modes through endpoint configuration policy rather than relying on user restraint.
Prevent simultaneous wired and wireless connections where the business case allows, or block forwarding between interfaces.
Deploy wireless intrusion detection that alerts on any unauthorised access point, not only on corporate SSID impersonation.
Enforce 802.1X on wired ports so that a bridged or plugged-in device cannot reach the network without authenticating.
Route endpoint traffic through an always-on tunnel so a tether does not remove monitoring visibility.
Address the underlying reason: where staff tether because coverage or filtering blocks legitimate work, fix that rather than only prohibiting the workaround.
WIFI-031.mitigationClientFacing: Company laptops can share their mobile data connection or bridge between networks, which creates a route into your network that bypasses your internet controls entirely — no filtering, no inspection, no record. Staff do this to work around poor coverage or a blocked site rather than to cause harm, which is worth knowing because it tells you where the pressure is. Disable the capability through your device management, and at the same time look at why it is being used: a network that works reliably and does not block things people legitimately need removes most of the motivation.

WIFI-032.prerequisites: A network using Device Provisioning Protocol onboarding, commonly deployed for headless IoT devices and increasingly for guest and staff onboarding by QR code. Physical or photographic access to a provisioning code, or the ability to place one. A wireless adapter with monitor mode for observing the exchange, and authorisation covering onboarding an unauthorised device.
WIFI-032.whatItIs: DPP replaces a shared passphrase with a public key exchanged out of band, usually as a QR code, and the cryptography is sound. The weakness is almost always in how the code is handled. A code printed on a label, displayed on a screen, or left in a shared document is a credential, and it is rarely treated as one. Anyone who photographs it can often enrol a device, because the bootstrapping key is the whole of the authorisation.
WIFI-032.rootCause: Deployment guidance focuses on the protocol rather than on the lifecycle of the code, so codes are commonly printed on device labels, posted in shared areas, or left in onboarding documentation. Many implementations accept the same code repeatedly instead of invalidating it after first use. Where a configurator role is delegated broadly, the number of people able to authorise a new device onto the network is larger than anyone intends.
WIFI-032.impact: A photographed or reused code lets an unauthorised device join the network with legitimate credentials, appearing in logs as a properly onboarded device rather than an intrusion. On an IoT segment that may be limited, but DPP is increasingly used for general access, where the consequence is a foothold on the corporate network. Because the enrolment is cryptographically valid, detection depends entirely on device inventory discipline rather than on any protocol-level signal.
stepsToIdentify: Establish where DPP is in use and for which device classes, since IoT and general access carry very different consequences.
Determine how bootstrapping codes are distributed: printed labels, screens, email, or a documentation system.
Check whether a code is invalidated after first successful use or remains valid indefinitely.
Identify who holds the configurator role and whether that is a small named set or a broad group.
Assess whether codes are ever rotated, particularly after a device is decommissioned or returned.
Review whether newly onboarded devices are reconciled against an approved inventory, and how quickly.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope permits onboarding a tester device and agree how it will be removed afterwards.
Locate a bootstrapping code through the normal environment: device labels, shared documentation, or a displayed screen.
Record how the code was obtained and whether any access control stood between the tester and it.
Attempt enrolment of a tester device using that code and observe whether it succeeds.
Attempt a second enrolment with the same code to establish whether single use is enforced.
Confirm what network access the enrolled device received, and whether its appearance triggered any alert.

variants: A code displayed on a screen in a public area such as a meeting room or reception, photographable by any visitor.
Codes stored in a shared onboarding document or ticketing system with broad read access.
A device returned or resold with its label intact, where the code remains valid against the original network.
Over-broad configurator delegation, where many staff can authorise devices and no approval step exists.
mitigation: Treat bootstrapping codes as credentials: control their distribution, avoid printing them where they can be photographed, and rotate them.
Enforce single use, invalidating a code once enrolment completes.
Restrict the configurator role to a small named set with an approval step for each enrolment.
Reconcile newly onboarded devices against an approved inventory and alert on any device that was not expected.
Place DPP-onboarded IoT devices on a dedicated segment with no route to corporate resources.
Invalidate codes as part of the decommissioning process so returned hardware cannot be used to rejoin.
WIFI-032.mitigationClientFacing: You are using the newer QR-code-based method of getting devices onto wireless, which is a sound approach and avoids sharing a password. The weakness found is in how the setup codes are handled: they can be reused, are not time-limited, and in some cases were found stored where others could see them. A code that stays valid is equivalent to the wireless password it replaces. Make the codes single-use with a short expiry, generate them per device rather than printing one for general use, and keep them out of shared documents and messages. This is a process change rather than a technology one.

WIFI-033.prerequisites: Wireless IoT or operational technology devices that expose their own access point for setup: cameras, sensors, controllers, building systems and similar. A wireless adapter for discovery and association. Authorisation to associate with device-hosted access points and interact with their provisioning interfaces, with a clear stop point before changing any device configuration.
WIFI-033.whatItIs: Most wireless IoT devices ship with a setup mode that broadcasts their own access point so a phone can configure them. The intent is that this mode closes once setup completes. In practice devices are frequently found still broadcasting it months later, either because provisioning never completed cleanly, or because the device re-enters setup mode after a power cycle, or because the firmware simply never disables it. That access point is usually open and its configuration interface usually unauthenticated.
WIFI-033.rootCause: Setup mode is designed for convenience during a one-time operation and the security posture reflects that: open network, no authentication, full configuration access. Manufacturers assume the window is brief and physically supervised. Devices are commonly installed by facilities contractors rather than IT, so nobody verifies afterwards that setup mode closed. Power cycles during maintenance frequently reopen it with no notification to anyone.
WIFI-033.impact: An open provisioning access point typically allows reading the stored wireless credentials the device uses for the production network, which yields the passphrase directly. It also permits reconfiguring the device to associate with an attacker-controlled network, and on operational technology it may expose control functions with safety consequences. Because these devices are rarely in the asset inventory, neither the exposure nor a subsequent compromise is likely to be noticed.
stepsToIdentify: Survey for access points whose SSIDs match manufacturer setup patterns, typically a vendor name with a serial or MAC fragment.
Identify the manufacturer from the BSSID prefix and the SSID naming convention.
Determine whether each provisioning access point is open or protected, and whether it is persistent across a power cycle.
Associate where permitted and identify the provisioning interface, usually a web service on the default gateway address.
Check whether the interface requires authentication, and whether any default credential is documented publicly.
Establish whether the stored production wireless credentials are readable through the interface.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers association and read-only interaction, and agree explicitly that no device configuration will be changed.
Survey during a walkthrough and record every device-hosted access point with its location.
Associate with one and enumerate the provisioning service on the assigned gateway address.
Access the configuration interface and record whether authentication was required at any point.
Where stored wireless credentials are exposed, capture the minimum evidence proving exposure without recording the passphrase in the report body.
Stop before modifying configuration, and report per device class since remediation is usually a firmware or process change across a fleet.

variants: Devices that re-enter setup mode automatically whenever they lose their configured network, making the exposure recurring.
Bluetooth-based provisioning with the same unauthenticated characteristics and no wireless survey footprint.
A cloud-paired device whose local provisioning interface remains active alongside the cloud channel.
Operational technology devices where the provisioning interface also exposes control functions with physical consequences.
mitigation: Verify after every installation that provisioning mode is closed, and make that a signed-off step in the commissioning checklist.
Require devices that re-enter setup mode to do so only after a deliberate physical action such as a button hold.
Place IoT and OT devices on a dedicated segment with no route to corporate resources, so exposed credentials reach nothing of value.
Use a wireless credential unique to the IoT segment, never one shared with corporate or guest networks.
Include wireless IoT devices in the asset inventory and in recurring wireless surveys, since they are usually installed outside IT's process.
Make provisioning security a procurement requirement: authenticated setup, a closing setup window, and no plaintext credential retrieval.
WIFI-033.mitigationClientFacing: Smart devices and operational equipment typically create their own temporary wireless network during setup so a phone can configure them. On several devices here that network is still running long after setup finished, and it accepts connections without a password. Anyone within range can connect and reconfigure the device. Check each device for whether this setup mode can be turned off after installation — most can, but it is rarely done because installation is usually carried out by a contractor with no instruction to do so. Add the step to your commissioning checklist, and place this equipment on its own network segment so a device that cannot be secured is at least contained.
